title: Browser AI Speedup: 200+ GPU Kernels Generated On the Fly, Not Precompiled
dek: In the browser, there is no 'universally optimal kernel': a kernel is the implementation of an operator on specific hardware, and different devices have different optima. The 200+ kernels are not hardcoded programs but templates that are generated in the browser for your device.
why: An 11-minute solo release demo, no back-and-forth, medium density. The point that kernels must be tailored to the device is made intuitively; worth a close look is the mechanism of templated kernels and Fleet's crowdsourced tuning.
who: Engineers running LLMs in the browser or building high-performance front-end AI applications, and technical decision-makers interested in WebGPU and WASM local inference solutions.
skip: The code walkthrough in the opening demo and the release channel introduction at the end can be sped through; focus on the kernel templating mechanism and the Fleet data feedback section.

points.h: Operators define, kernels run on hardware
points.body: The transcript first distinguishes two concepts: a model is a large graph of operators; an operator is just a mathematical definition—addition is A+B. A kernel, on the other hand, is the implementation that brings that definition to specific hardware. The same add, in the browser, goes through WebGPU/WGSL; in other ecosystems, it corresponds to a CUDA or Metal kernel. The two are often conflated, but the speed difference comes precisely from the latter: if the underlying kernel is fast, the whole inference graph can be fast. This also explains why it's worth polishing a kernel for a simple operation repeatedly, rather than vaguely tuning a 'general math library'.

points.h: What's shipped is Jinja templates, not hardcoded kernels
points.body: The difference in approach is worth noting: the repo doesn't contain hardcoded WGSL files one by one, but several Jinja templates that use if/else to describe branches for different devices. At execution, the library validates the template, selects the appropriate data type and workgroup size, and renders the WGSL most suitable for the current GPU adapter to run. For example, the same addition function: on the left, the data type is narrow and the workgroup size is small; on the right, because the device supports wider data types and larger workgroups, the same add runs faster. The official release lists 200+ kernel entries, but what's actually delivered is the ability to 'make kernels on the fly for the hardware'.

points.h: Attention in the browser takes only about 20 lines of JS
points.body: The demo brings abstraction back to reality: running a small attention mechanism in the browser took only about 20 lines of JavaScript. The flow is text → token → vector, but a token's vector cannot be viewed in isolation; you have to see how other tokens in the context affect it. The code only calls in four kernels from the Hub—matmul, softmax, add, layer normalization—and the rest of the scheduling and GPU data exchange is hidden by the Hugging Face Kernels library. The heavy lifting is all at the kernel layer; that's why the barrier to 'doing local inference in the browser' has dropped.

points.h: The entire wave animation is just one matrix multiplication
points.body: The same demo gives an intuitive comparison: 128 waves pass through a 1024×1024 matrix, and each cell's color is an RGBA computed by a matrix multiplication. The animation of over a million pixels runs at about 60fps under WebGPU—60 is not the compute limit; it's just that requestAnimationFrame locks rendering to 60, while the kernel itself can compute at about 400fps. Running the same logic in plain JavaScript yields roughly 6.75fps. The gap isn't in the math, but in whether someone has written an implementation that hugs this particular GPU—that's what those kernels do.

points.h: Fleet turns user devices into tuning data via tests
points.body: Fleet is ostensibly a benchmark page: anyone can run their own GPU and see how it performs in comparison. But the team puts it bluntly: they only have a few devices of their own, while the real world has thousands of WebGPU devices, possibly with edge cases they haven't thought of—some kernels might perform poorly on your machine, or even fail outright. Fleet collects runtime data from real devices to continue optimization, and the improved kernels, being open source, return to all users. When you click 'Run Benchmark', you're not just seeing a score; you're also doing a round of real-environment adaptation testing for the project.

terms.def: The implementation of an operator on specific hardware; the same addition requires different kernels on different GPUs.
WebGPU Shading Language, the language for writing kernels in the WebGPU environment; it's the bridge to the GPU in the browser.
A Python template engine; Hugging Face uses .jinja files to describe kernels, then renders them to WGSL at runtime based on the device.
The next-generation API for accessing the GPU from the browser; the computational foundation for local AI inference in the browser.
